items.hint1: The word 'but' tells you the chairman's view is the reverse of what many people thought. Before looking at the options, pin down exactly what the underlined word means.
items.hint2: Be careful: invaluable does not mean 'not valuable'. It means so valuable that no price could be put on it. So the gap needs a word for having no value or no use at all.
items.hint3: Insincere is about honesty and impossible is about whether something can happen, so neither is about worth. Choose between the other two by asking which one means 'of no value'.
items.solution:
Answer: B. useless

In an antonym question the gap must hold the word most nearly opposite in meaning to the underlined word. Invaluable means extremely valuable, worth more than any price, even though it begins with in-. Its opposite is a word meaning of no value or no use.

How to tell: many people saw Abdul's contribution as very valuable, and 'but' shows the chairman took the opposite view. A contribution with no value is useless.

Why not the others:
A. insincere: this is about honesty, not about value.
C. impossible: this is about whether something can happen, not about worth.
D. preposterous: this means foolish or absurd, a judgement of sense rather than of value.

Exam tip: check the exact meaning of the underlined word before choosing its opposite. Words such as invaluable and priceless look negative but mean very valuable, so their opposites are words like useless and worthless.

items.hint1: The word 'but' sets up a contrast between the two brothers. Think about where you usually meet the underlined word: in talk about blame and wrongdoing.
items.hint2: Culpable means deserving blame for something wrong, in other words guilty. Accountable means answerable for something, which is close to culpable, so it cannot be the opposite.
items.hint3: Ignorant is about lack of knowledge, not blame. Of the two left, which one means free from blame, rather than just a good quality of character?
items.solution:
Answer: A. innocent

An antonym must be opposite in the same area of meaning as the underlined word. Culpable means guilty or deserving blame, so its opposite is a word meaning not guilty, free from blame.

How to tell: the sentence says one boy may be to blame, but his brother is surely not. The word for someone who has done no wrong is innocent.

Why not the others:
B. ignorant: this means lacking knowledge, which has nothing to do with blame.
C. accountable: this means answerable for something, which is close to culpable, not opposite to it.
D. honest: this is a good quality of character, but an honest person can still be to blame for something.

Exam tip: in antonym questions, watch for an option that is a near-synonym of the underlined word, because examiners plant one. Then choose the opposite that stays in the same area of meaning, here guilt against innocence.

items.hint1: The sentence contrasts how the teacher used to be with how he is now. Work out what being rigid in your opinions means, then check which word fits before 'of other people's views'.
items.hint2: Rigid in your opinions means fixed, unwilling to change your views or accept other ideas. Apprise is a verb meaning to inform, so it cannot describe a person in this gap.
items.hint3: Three adjectives remain. Ask which one is about accepting views that differ from your own, rather than doubting them or finding fault with them.
items.solution:
Answer: D. tolerant

The opposite of being rigid in your opinions is being open to other people's opinions. A person who accepts views different from their own is tolerant of them.

How to tell: the teacher 'used to be' fixed in his opinions, and 'but he is now' signals the reverse. 'Tolerant of other people's views' is also a correct phrase, so the word fits both the meaning and the grammar.

Why not the others:
A. wary: this means cautious or suspicious, which is not the same as accepting views different from your own.
B. critical: finding fault with other views is not the reverse of being fixed in your own.
C. apprise: this is a verb meaning to inform, so it cannot follow 'he is now' as a description.

Exam tip: test the chosen word in the full sentence. The right antonym must also be the right word class and must go with the words after the gap, as in 'tolerant of'.

items.hint1: The contrast is between the workers and their leader. Find the meaning of the underlined word first, and note that the gap after 'was rather' needs an adjective.
items.hint2: Affable means friendly, pleasant and easy to talk to. Caution is a noun, so it cannot follow 'was rather'.
items.hint3: Guarded and suspicious both describe being careful with people. Ask which remaining option shows open hostility, as strong in the unfriendly direction as affable is in the friendly one.
items.solution:
Answer: D. antagonistic

The best antonym reverses the core meaning of the underlined word. Affable means warm and friendly, so its opposite is a word meaning hostile or unfriendly.

How to tell: some workers were friendly, 'but' their leader was the reverse. Antagonistic means showing hostility or opposition towards others, the direct opposite of friendly.

Why not the others:
A. guarded: this means careful about what you say, which is not the same as unfriendly.
B. caution: this is a noun, so it does not fit the gap, and it means care, not hostility.
C. suspicious: this means distrustful, which is not the direct opposite of friendly.

Exam tip: when several options are mildly negative, choose the one that reverses the main meaning of the underlined word with the same strength, and reject any option of the wrong word class.

items.hint1: The driver expected one reaction and got the reverse. Work out what kind of action the underlined word describes: is it something done with words, a legal step, or a physical act?
items.hint2: Castigated means scolded or criticised severely. Released and encouraged do not reverse harsh criticism, so set them aside.
items.hint3: Exonerated and commended both sound positive. One means cleared of a charge or blame, the other means praised. Which is the reverse of being scolded?
items.solution:
Answer: C. commended

An antonym should reverse the same kind of action. Castigated means severely scolded or criticised, an action done with words, so its opposite is being praised.

How to tell: the driver feared harsh criticism from the passengers, but 'but' shows he got the reverse. To commend someone is to praise them.

Why not the others:
A. encouraged: this means given hope or confidence, which is not the reverse of being scolded.
B. exonerated: this means cleared of a charge or blame, so it is the opposite of accused, not of scolded.
D. released: this means set free, the opposite of held or arrested.

Exam tip: match the kind of action when choosing an opposite: criticise against praise, accuse against clear, arrest against release. Two options can both look positive, but only one reverses the same action.

items.hint1: Note both what the underlined word means and how strong it is. In antonym questions the best answer usually matches the strength of the underlined word.
items.hint2: Eulogized means praised very highly, usually in public. Apprised means informed, and discourage is the wrong form to follow 'was'.
items.hint3: Criticized and denounced both go against praise. Which one matches the strength and the public nature of eulogized?
items.solution:
Answer: D. denounced

When two options are both opposites, the examiner rewards the one that matches the strength of the underlined word. Eulogized means praised very highly and publicly, so its best opposite is a word for strong public condemnation.

How to tell: to denounce someone is to condemn them openly and strongly. That mirrors eulogize in both strength and public character, while criticize is milder.

Why not the others:
A. discourage: this base form does not fit after 'was', and it means to reduce someone's confidence, not to condemn.
B. criticized: this does oppose praise, but it is milder than the high praise in eulogized.
C. apprised: this means informed, which has nothing to do with praise or blame.

Exam tip: if two options are both opposites, pick the one equal in strength. High praise pairs with strong condemnation, and mild praise pairs with mild criticism.

items.hint1: Think about what quality the underlined word describes: is it about giving, or about feelings? The opposite must describe the same quality.
items.hint2: Generous means willing to give freely, sharing money, time or things. Sympathetic is a kindly quality, so it is closer to generous than opposite to it.
items.hint3: Nasty and mean can both describe unkindness, but only one of them can also mean unwilling to give or share. Which is it?
items.solution:
Answer: D. mean

The opposite of generous must describe the same quality, giving, in reverse. In British English, which WAEC follows, mean describing a person can mean unwilling to give or spend, in other words stingy.

How to tell: some people give freely to strangers, while 'while' marks others as the reverse. People who do not like to give or share are mean.

Why not the others:
A. indifferent: this means not caring, and an indifferent person could still give.
B. sympathetic: this means caring about others' feelings, which is close to generous.
C. nasty: this means unpleasant or unkind in general, not unwilling to give.

Exam tip: some words have more than one meaning. Mean can be unkind, stingy or average. In antonym questions, use the meaning that reverses the underlined word.

items.hint1: The baby changed suddenly from one state to its reverse. Think about what being calm looks like, then picture the opposite.
items.hint2: Calm means quiet, still and settled. Hungry names a need of the body, not a state of calm or disturbance, and cheerful can go together with calm.
items.hint3: Angry and restless both describe losing calm. Which is the direct reverse of being quiet and settled, rather than one particular emotion?
items.solution:
Answer: A. restless

The best antonym describes the same kind of state in reverse. Calm means quiet, still and settled, so its opposite is agitated and unable to keep still or settle.

How to tell: a baby that had been calm and suddenly cannot settle, keeps moving and fusses has become restless, which is exactly the reverse of calm.

Why not the others:
B. hungry: this is a need that may cause restlessness, but it is not the opposite of calm.
C. angry: this names one emotion, while the opposite of calm is being unsettled in general.
D. cheerful: this is a happy mood, which can go together with being calm.

Exam tip: choose the opposite that describes the same kind of state. Calm is about being still and settled, so look for words like restless, agitated or troubled rather than a named feeling or a bodily need.

items.hint1: Here the gap comes first and the underlined word comes last. The underlined word (self-effacing, misprinted in the paper) breaks into 'self' and 'efface', which means to rub out.
items.hint2: Self-effacing means modest, keeping yourself in the background and not drawing attention to yourself. Lousy is informal for very bad or poor, and it does not describe how someone sees themselves.
items.hint3: Aggressive and conceited are the strongest remaining choices. One is about attacking others, the other about how highly you rate yourself. Which reverses modesty?
items.solution:
Answer: C. conceited

Self-effacing (printed in the paper as 'self-effacting') describes a modest person who keeps in the background. Its opposite describes a person who thinks too highly of themselves.

How to tell: 'while' contrasts Ade with his wife. If she is modest, he is the reverse: conceited, meaning vain and full of his own importance.

Why not the others:
A. aggressive: this means ready to attack or quarrel, which is about behaviour towards others, not about modesty.
B. lousy: this is an informal word for very bad, and it is not about how a person sees themselves.
D. unfriendly: this is about warmth towards others, and a modest person can be unfriendly too.

Exam tip: when the underlined word describes how a person sees themselves, keep the opposite in the same field: self-effacing or modest against conceited, vain or arrogant.

items.hint1: When the underlined word describes a husband, it often refers to how he handles money and decisions. Decide which sense fits before you look for the opposite.
items.hint2: Prudent means careful and sensible, especially with money. Thoughtful is close to prudent in meaning, so it is not the opposite.
items.hint3: A prudent husband is careful with money. Of the options left, which one describes a husband who spends money freely and wastefully, the reverse of careful?
items.solution:
Answer: B. extravagant

Prudent means careful and sensible, especially in spending money. Its opposite describes someone who spends carelessly and wastefully.

How to tell: 'while' contrasts the two husbands. If Bakary manages money carefully, the reverse is a husband who spends far more than is wise, and that is extravagant.

Why not the others:
A. mean: this means stingy, unwilling to spend, which is careful with money taken too far, so it is closer to prudent than opposite.
C. thoughtful: this means careful and considerate, which is close to prudent in meaning.
D. mindless: this means without thought, which is too general and not about money.

Exam tip: when the underlined word has a money sense, look for the opposite in the same field: prudent or thrifty against extravagant or wasteful.

items.hint1: This sentence uses the language of elections. Think of the phrase used for the difference in votes between the winner and the person who came second.
items.hint2: Consensus means general agreement, and space means room or distance. Neither describes a difference in votes.
items.hint3: Surplus and margin both involve an amount. Which one is used in the phrase 'won by a ... of twenty votes'?
items.solution:
Answer: D. margin

In election language, the margin is the difference in votes between the winner and the runner-up. You win 'by a margin of' so many votes.

How to tell: the chairman won by twenty votes more than his rival. That difference is his margin of victory.

Why not the others:
A. surplus: this is an amount left over beyond what is needed, used of money, food or goods, not a vote difference.
B. consensus: this means general agreement among a group, not a count of votes.
C. space: this means room or distance, not a number of votes.

Exam tip: learn register words in the phrases they go with: win by a margin, cast a vote, a landslide victory, the incumbent chairman.

items.hint1: This is the language of meetings. The word 'dismissed' in the first part of the sentence is a misprint for 'discussed'. Think about what a chairman does to a meeting once its business is done.
items.hint2: 'Dismissed' is used mostly for sending people away, such as a class or a worker, or for rejecting a court case; it is not the usual word for formally closing a meeting. Suspended means paused for a while, to carry on later, which clashes with 'all items had been discussed'.
items.hint3: Dissolved and adjourned are both used of meetings and official bodies. One ends a body such as a parliament or committee for good; the other closes a single sitting. Which fits one meeting whose agenda is done?
items.solution:
Answer: C. adjourned

In the language of meetings, when all the business is finished the chairman adjourns the meeting, that is, formally brings the sitting to a close, usually until the next meeting. (The paper printed 'dismissed' where it meant 'discussed'.)

How to tell: every item on the agenda had been dealt with, so the meeting was formally closed. The word used for that is adjourned.

Why not the others:
A. dismissed: this is used mostly for sending people away or rejecting a case, and it is not the usual word for formally closing a meeting.
B. suspended: this means paused for a while, to carry on later, which does not fit a meeting whose business is all done.
D. dissolved: this means ending a body such as a parliament or committee, not closing one sitting.

Exam tip: learn the meeting register as a set: agenda, quorum, motion, minutes, adjourn. When a word looks close, ask whether it applies to one sitting or to the whole body.

items.hint1: This is the language of law. An aggrieved person is someone who has been wronged. Think about what such a person goes to court to get.
items.hint2: Address can mean a speech or where someone lives, and restoration means bringing something back to its old state, as with a building or order. Neither is the legal word used with 'seek' here.
items.hint3: Litigation and redress are both legal words. One is the process of taking a case to court; the other is the remedy a wronged person hopes to receive. Which one do you seek in court?
items.solution:
Answer: A. redress

In legal language, redress is a remedy or compensation for a wrong done to you. People who have been wronged 'seek redress', usually in a court of law.

How to tell: the aggrieved persons want the wrong put right, and they go to court to get it. What they seek is redress.

Why not the others:
B. litigation: this is the process of taking legal action itself, not the remedy a person seeks from the court.
C. address: this is a speech or a place where someone lives, and it only looks like redress.
D. restoration: this means bringing something back to an earlier state, and it is not the fixed legal term here.

Exam tip: learn legal register words with the verbs they go with: seek redress, file a suit, grant bail, pass judgement. Watch for options that only look like the answer, such as address and redress.

items.hint1: The gap needs a collective noun, a word for a group. Different animals have different group words.
items.hint2: A skein is a group of geese in flight, and a gang is usually a group of people, such as workers or thieves.
items.hint3: Flock and herd are both used for farm animals. Which one goes with cows, and which with sheep and goats?
items.solution:
Answer: B. herd

A collective noun names a group, and many kinds of animal have their own group word. The usual collective noun for cows and cattle is herd.

How to tell: the principal owns many cows, so the phrase is 'a large herd of cows'.

Why not the others:
A. gang: this is usually used for a group of people, such as labourers or thieves.
C. skein: this is used for geese flying together.
D. flock: this is used for sheep, goats and birds, not cows.

Exam tip: learn collective nouns in pairs: a herd of cattle, a flock of sheep, a pride of lions, a swarm of bees, a shoal of fish.

items.hint1: 'Stands as a historic ...' is about what the building represents, not only what it is. Think of the word that goes with 'historic' for something kept to remind people of the past.
items.hint2: An effigy is a model or image of a person, and an artefact is usually a handmade object, such as a tool or pot kept in a museum. Neither is the usual word for a landmark building.
items.hint3: Edifice and monument can both describe a building. One simply means a large, grand building; the other means a structure valued as a reminder of history. Which fits 'stands as a historic'?
items.solution:
Answer: C. monument

A monument is a structure kept and valued because it reminds people of an important person or event in history. 'Historic monument' is the phrase used for such a structure.

How to tell: the building is important because it was the first of its kind, and 'stands as' shows it represents that history. That is what a monument does.

Why not the others:
A. effigy: this is a model or likeness of a person, not a building.
B. artefact: this usually names a handmade object, such as a tool or pot, not a landmark building.
D. edifice: this means a large, imposing building, which only repeats that it is a building and says nothing about its history.

Exam tip: when two options both fit the literal meaning, choose the one that fits the whole phrase and adds meaning, as in 'historic monument', rather than one that repeats a word already in the sentence.

items.hint1: The gap is paired with 'refreshed'. Think of a word describing how a person feels after a good rest: full of new energy.
items.hint2: Reloaded is used of guns, machines or computer programs, and remodeled is used of buildings or designs, not of how a person feels.
items.hint3: Revived and rejuvenated both mean given new life. One is a general word for getting back strength or energy; the other adds the idea of feeling young and full of energy again. Which gives the fuller picture, alongside 'refreshed', of how a holiday leaves you?
items.solution:
Answer: A. rejuvenated

To be rejuvenated is to feel young and full of energy again. It is the natural partner of 'refreshed' when describing someone after a rest or holiday.

How to tell: the speaker came back from a vacation feeling renewed in body and mind. 'Refreshed and rejuvenated' describes exactly that.

Why not the others:
B. revived: this is a general word for getting back strength or energy, and it does not carry the sense of feeling young again that 'rejuvenated' adds, so it is the weaker partner for 'refreshed' here.
C. reloaded: this is used of guns, machines or software, not of a person's state.
D. remodeled: this is used of buildings or designs being changed, not of people.

Exam tip: ask what kind of thing a word normally describes, a person, a machine or a building. The right word fits both the meaning and the kind of subject in the sentence.

items.hint1: This is the language of health. Many specialist doctors are named after the part of the body or the group of patients they treat, and the first part of each name is the clue.
items.hint2: A cardiologist treats the heart ('cardio' refers to the heart), so it does not fit a skin disease.
items.hint3: Of the three left, one treats health problems of women, one treats the eyes and one treats the skin. Look at the start of each word to decide.
items.solution:
Answer: B. dermatologist

Many specialist doctors are named from a Greek root for the body part they treat. 'Derma' means skin, so a dermatologist treats diseases of the skin.

How to tell: she had an unusual skin disease, so she needed the specialist for skin.

Why not the others:
A. cardiologist: this doctor treats the heart.
C. gynaecologist: this doctor treats women's reproductive health.
D. ophthalmologist: this doctor treats the eyes.

Exam tip: learn the roots and you can name many specialists: cardio (heart), derma (skin), ophthalm (eye), neuro (nerves), paed (children), and -logist means a specialist.

items.hint1: The sentence tells us what the doctor decided the patient was suffering from. Think about the medical word for that decision.
items.hint2: A prescription is the medicine or treatment a doctor orders, and a prediction is a statement about what will happen in the future.
items.hint3: Analysis and diagnosis both involve examining. Which is the doctor's conclusion that names the disease, and which is the general process of examining something in detail?
items.solution:
Answer: C. diagnosis

A diagnosis is a doctor's identification of the illness a patient has, made from symptoms and tests.

How to tell: the doctor concluded that the patient was suffering from cancer. Naming the disease is the diagnosis.

Why not the others:
A. prediction: this is about what will happen in the future, not what the patient has now.
B. prescription: this is the medicine or treatment ordered after the illness is known.
D. analysis: this is a detailed examination of something, not the doctor's conclusion naming the disease.

Exam tip: learn health register in the order it happens: symptoms, diagnosis (naming the illness), prescription (ordering treatment), prognosis (the likely outcome).

items.hint1: The phrase 'to make him work harder' tells you the purpose of the gift. Look for the word for something given to encourage effort.
items.hint2: Interest means wanting to know about something, or money paid on a loan, and an attraction is something that draws people, such as a tourist site.
items.hint3: Offer and incentive remain. Reread the purpose, 'to make him work harder', and ask which of the two words is defined by that kind of purpose.
items.solution:
Answer: A. incentive

An incentive is something given or promised to encourage a person to act or to work harder.

How to tell: Tom's father gave him something valuable so that he would work harder in school. A gift given for that purpose is an incentive.

Why not the others:
B. attraction: this is something that draws people towards it, not a reward for effort.
C. interest: this means curiosity about something, or money paid on a loan.
D. offer: this is something put forward for someone to accept or refuse, and it does not carry the idea of motivating effort.

Exam tip: read the purpose clause ('to make him', 'so that', 'in order to'). It usually tells you exactly what the missing word must do.

items.hint1: The gap completes a common phrase you hear on radio and television about tomorrow's weather.
items.hint2: A broadcast is a programme sent out on radio or television, and an announcement is any public statement. Neither is the usual name for the report about coming weather.
items.hint3: Prediction and forecast both mean saying what will happen. Which one is the fixed word that goes with 'weather'?
items.solution:
Answer: A. forecast

A forecast is a statement of what is likely to happen, based on information. 'Weather forecast' is the fixed phrase for the report on coming weather.

How to tell: people 'hear the weather forecast' on radio or television. The other words do not form this set phrase with 'weather'.

Why not the others:
B. broadcast: this is a programme sent out on radio or television, not the usual name for the weather report itself.
C. prediction: this has a similar meaning, but 'weather forecast' is the set phrase.
D. announcement: this is a general public statement, too broad for the weather report.

Exam tip: some words are fixed partners. When two options mean nearly the same, choose the one that forms the recognised phrase: weather forecast, heavy rain, strong wind.

items.hint1: Focus on the expression 'jangle the old man's nerve(s)'. Think about how a person feels when their nerves are shaken.
items.hint2: To jangle someone's nerves is to upset them and make them feel nervous or on edge. Harass and tease both mean deliberately troubling someone or making fun of them, which the expression does not require.
items.hint3: Annoy and disturb both fit loosely. One means only to irritate; the other covers upsetting someone's peace and making them uneasy. Which fits the word 'nerves'?
items.solution:
Answer: C. disturb the old man

To jangle someone's nerves is to unsettle them, making them nervous, upset or on edge. The option that covers that whole feeling is to disturb them. (The paper printed 'Oja' and 'nerve' as slips for 'Ojo' and 'nerves'.)

How to tell: Ojo was warned not to shake the old man's calm. Disturbing someone means breaking their peace and making them uneasy, which matches the expression.

Why not the others:
A. harass the old man: this means troubling someone deliberately and repeatedly, which the expression does not say.
B. annoy the old man: this captures only irritation and misses the nervous unease that 'nerves' carries.
D. tease the old man: this means making fun of someone, which is not what the expression means.

Exam tip: in 'This means that' questions, when several options are close, pick the one that covers the whole meaning of the expression, not just one part of it.

items.hint1: This is an idiom about a strong feeling on first meeting someone. Do not read it as something that happened to her feet.
items.hint2: The idiom describes a sudden, powerful feeling towards a person. Becoming confused and trusting someone completely are not what it describes.
items.hint3: Being pleasantly surprised and falling in love both describe a good feeling. Which one matches the strength of 'completely swept off her feet'?
items.solution:
Answer: A. fell deeply in love

To be swept off your feet is an idiom meaning to fall suddenly and deeply in love with someone, as if the feeling lifted you off the ground.

How to tell: 'completely swept off her feet the first time she met Gabriel' describes Amina falling strongly in love with him at once.

Why not the others:
B. was pleasantly surprised: this is far too weak and misses the romantic meaning.
C. trusted him completely: trust is not what the idiom describes.
D. became utterly confused: the idiom is about attraction, not confusion.

Exam tip: an idiom's meaning is not the sum of its words. Picture the image, here being lifted off the ground by a strong feeling, and pick the option that matches both its sense and its strength.

items.hint1: 'Abreast' means side by side, level with. Think about what it means to keep level with events as they happen.
items.hint2: Keeping abreast is about knowledge, not action. Being involved in events means taking part in them, which the expression does not say.
items.hint3: Mindful, curious and well-informed all involve attention. Which one says he actually has up-to-date knowledge, rather than only caring about events or wanting to know?
items.solution:
Answer: C. well-informed about events

To keep abreast of something is to stay up to date with it, knowing the latest news and developments.

How to tell: his response showed that he knew what was happening in the country. A person who knows the latest news is well-informed.

Why not the others:
A. mindful of events: this means aware of or careful about events, not up to date with them.
B. involved in events: this means taking part, while the expression is about knowing.
D. curious about events: this means wanting to know, not already knowing.

Exam tip: for 'This means that' idioms, separate knowing, feeling and doing. Choose the option that matches the kind of meaning the expression carries.

items.hint1: Picture the buildings on that road standing in a line, and count from the end.
items.hint2: In 'last but one', the word 'but' means 'except'. So the phrase means last if you leave one out. Options that put the school at the very end, or beyond the end, cannot be right.
items.hint3: Two options remain. Count back from the end: find the last building, then step back one place. Which option names where you now stand?
items.solution:
Answer: D. the one before the last

'The last but one' means second from the end. Here 'but' is used in its sense of 'except': it is the last, except for one building after it.

How to tell: count from the end of the road. The last building is number one from the end, so the last but one is the building just before it.

Why not the others:
A. the very last building: that would be 'the last', not 'the last but one'.
B. one of the last building: this is vague, and the expression gives one exact position.
C. the one after the last: nothing comes after the last building on the road.

Exam tip: in expressions such as 'the last but one' or 'all but one', read 'but' as 'except'. Then count to find the exact position or number.

items.hint1: This idiom is about how something looks. Think about what makes a thing 'easy' for your eyes.
items.hint2: The idiom is about how pleasant something is to look at, not its price. Cool is informal and too vague for this meaning, and expensive is about cost.
items.hint3: Grandiose and attractive both describe appearance. One means pleasing to look at; the other means very large and showy, often too much. Which fits 'easy on the eye'?
items.solution:
Answer: C. attractive

If something is easy on the eye, it is pleasant to look at. The plain word for that is attractive.

How to tell: a plaza that your eyes enjoy looking at is a good-looking, attractive building.

Why not the others:
A. grandiose: this means very large, grand and showy, often too much so; it is about size and show, not about being pleasant to look at.
B. cool: this is informal and too vague, and it can refer to temperature.
D. expensive: this is about cost, not appearance.

Exam tip: many idioms use a body part to point to a sense. 'Easy on the eye' is about sight and 'easy on the ear' is about sound, so match the option to the sense the idiom names.

items.hint1: This is an idiom. 'Thick' and 'thin' stand for two opposite kinds of situation in life.
items.hint2: The idiom is about loyalty over time, not about travelling together or giving advice. So accompanying you everywhere and always advising you are off the point.
items.hint3: Two options remain. Which one is about loyalty to a person, rather than readiness for events?
items.solution:
Answer: B. stand by you in good and bad times

'Through thick and thin' means in all conditions, good and bad. A friend who is with you through thick and thin stays loyal whatever happens.

How to tell: the sentence describes what a good friend does. Staying loyal in both good and difficult times is what the idiom means.

Why not the others:
A. be prepared for any eventually: this is about readiness for events, not loyalty to a friend.
C. accompany you anywhere you go: this takes 'with you' too literally, as physical travel.
D. always advise you: giving advice is not what the idiom describes.

Exam tip: idioms built on a pair of opposites, such as thick and thin, ups and downs, or rain or shine, usually mean 'in all conditions'.

items.hint1: This is an idiom, so do not take it literally. It describes how a person is feeling.
items.hint2: The idiom has nothing to do with rain or travel, so the literal options about rain and being outside the country are traps.
items.hint3: Sad and ill remain. Decide whether the idiom describes a person's mood or their health.
items.solution:
Answer: B. ill

'Under the weather' is an idiom meaning unwell, usually mildly ill.

How to tell: Willy has been feeling unwell for some days. That is what being under the weather means.

Why not the others:
A. sad: the idiom is about health, not mood.
C. in the rain: this is a literal reading of 'weather', which is the trap.
D. outside the country: nothing in the idiom refers to travel.

Exam tip: in idiom questions, an option that takes the words literally, such as rain for 'weather', is usually a trap. Look for the figurative meaning.

items.hint1: This is an idiom. 'His own game' refers to the way a person usually does things or wins.
items.hint2: The idiom is about how he lost, not about missing a target or forgetting how to play.
items.hint3: Two options remain, both about Taya's tactics. Ask: does the idiom say his tactics were revealed to others, or that someone used them against him?
items.solution:
Answer: D. Taya’s method were used to defeat him

To be beaten at your own game means to be defeated by someone using your own methods or tricks, often in the very thing you are known to be good at.

How to tell: 'his own game' is Taya's usual way of winning, and 'beaten at' it means someone else used that way against him and won.

Why not the others:
A. Taya’s strategies were leaked: the idiom says nothing about his plans being revealed.
B. Taya’s missed the target: the idiom is about being defeated by his own methods, not about missing.
C. Taya’s forgot his own tactics: the idiom is not about forgetting; it means someone else used his tactics against him.

Exam tip: for idioms about defeat, ask how the person lost and whose methods were used. 'Beaten at your own game' and 'hoist with your own petard' both mean your own plan was turned against you.

items.hint1: The key words are 'pull through'. It is a verb followed by a small word, and together they have a meaning different from 'pull'.
items.hint2: Pull through is about the outcome of an illness. It has nothing to do with gaining immunity or how long the illness lasted.
items.hint3: Two opposite outcomes remain. Work out which outcome 'pull through' describes, then keep 'did not believe that he would' in front of it.
items.solution:
Answer: A. recover from the sickness

To pull through an illness means to survive it and get better.

How to tell: the family never believed Father would pull through the fever, so they did not believe he would recover. The negative stays in the frame of the sentence, and the gap takes the plain meaning of 'pull through'.

Why not the others:
B. acquire immunity to the fever: pull through means surviving the illness, not becoming protected from it.
C. die from the sickness: this is the reverse of pulling through.
D. suffer so long: the expression is about the outcome, not the length of the illness.

Exam tip: when a 'This means that' sentence contains a negative, first find the meaning of the expression, then check that the option fits the frame after the negative. The trap option is often the exact reverse.
items.placement_challenge: idioms.phrasal-verbs: the sentence turns on 'pull through', a verb and particle meaning recover, and the taxonomy sends 'the meaning of a phrasal verb' there; idioms.idioms is defensible only through its 'This means that' format rule.

items.hint1: Decide what job the marked word does in the sentence. Does it describe something a person did, or how clear a fact was? Its partner must do the same job.
items.hint2: Here, apparent means plain or clear to see. Test each option by asking: does it describe how clear the fact was, or an action that someone carried out?
items.hint3: Narrow it to noticed and evident. Put each one in place of the marked word and ask which reads as a description of the fact itself, without needing a person who did something.
items.solution:
Answer: B. evident

Apparent here means clear or plain for anyone to see. It describes how obvious a fact is, so the word nearest in meaning must also describe a fact as clear.

How to tell: the sentence says the fact that John damaged the desk was plain to see. Evident means exactly that: clear and easy to see or understand. Swap it in and the meaning stays the same.

Why not the others:
A. noticed: this is something a person does, seeing or becoming aware of something, not a word for how clear a fact is.
C. recognized: this is also an act by a person, knowing or accepting something, not a word meaning clear.
D. acknowledged: this means admitted or accepted as true, which someone does; it says nothing about how obvious the fact was.

Exam tip: first decide whether the marked word names an action or describes a quality. Then swap each option into the sentence and keep the one that leaves the meaning unchanged.

items.hint1: Think about what customs officers have the power to do with goods at a border, and what the marked word says happened to the goods in the end.
items.hint2: To impound something is to take it away officially and keep it. An option that only means checked or slowed down does not cover the taking and keeping.
items.hint3: Two options are left, intercepted and confiscated. Both can involve officers stopping goods. Decide which one also carries the idea of taking and keeping from hint 2.
items.solution:
Answer: C. confiscated

To impound goods is to take them away by official power and keep them, as customs officers or the police can do. Confiscate means the same thing: to take something from someone by authority.

How to tell: the sentence is about customs officers acting on a merchant's goods. Impounded goods are no longer with the owner, they are held by the officers. Confiscated gives that same end result.

Why not the others:
A. intercepted: means stopped or caught on the way; intercepted goods can still be checked and released to the owner.
B. delayed: means held up or made late, not officially taken away and kept.
D. screened: means checked or inspected, not taken away.

Exam tip: for words about official action (impound, seize, detain, confiscate), ask what happens to the thing at the end. Choose the option with the same end result, not just the same first step.

items.hint1: Think of where else you have met the marked word, for example when people talk about the moon. Then ask whether it describes something getting less bit by bit or vanishing completely.
items.hint2: To wane is to grow gradually smaller or weaker. The right option must mean becoming less, not being gone altogether.
items.hint3: Two options suggest the trust ended completely, which is more than waning. Of the two left, one is about getting worse in condition and the other is about getting less. Which fits trust that is shrinking?
items.solution:
Answer: D. decrease

To wane is to become gradually smaller, weaker or less, like the moon after it is full. The word nearest in meaning must describe a going down in amount or strength, not a complete loss.

How to tell: the trust started to become less. The word suddenly tells you when this began, not that the trust vanished at once. Decrease means to become less, which matches wane in both meaning and strength.

Why not the others:
A. dissipate: means to scatter and fade away until gone, which is stronger than wane.
B. disappear: means to go completely out of sight or existence, but trust that is waning is still there, only less.
C. deteriorate: means to become worse in condition or quality, like a road or someone's health, while wane is about growing less.

Exam tip: when several options seem close, check the degree and the kind of change. Choose the option that matches the strength of the marked word, not a stronger one such as gone completely.

items.hint1: Think about what people who hold this belief fear when they see such a bird on a roof. The marked word is about what the sight is taken to mean.
items.hint2: Ominous describes a sign that something bad is about to happen. The right option must carry both ideas: a sign of the future, and a bad one. Options about rules or about distrust carry neither.
items.hint3: You should be left with prophetic and portentous. Both look to the future. Which one also carries the sense of warning or misfortune?
items.solution:
Answer: B. portentous

Ominous means giving a sign that something bad is going to happen. In this sense, portentous means the same: acting as a warning sign of something, usually bad, to come.

How to tell: the belief is that an owl on the roof is a bad sign for the people in the house. The word you want must include both the idea of a sign and the idea of something bad. Portentous has both.

Why not the others:
A. forbidden: means not allowed, which is about a rule, not a sign.
C. prophetic: means correctly telling what will happen, good or bad, so it does not carry the sense of danger.
D. suspicious: means causing distrust or doubting someone, not giving a sign of future trouble.

Exam tip: if the marked word carries a feeling, good or bad, its partner must carry the same feeling. Knock out options that share only the neutral part of the meaning.

items.hint1: Picture the town from above. The marked word tells you which part of the town the mall stands in.
items.hint2: A fringe is the outer border of something, like the fringe on a piece of cloth. The mall is still in the town, so the answer must name a part of the town, not a place beyond it.
items.hint3: One option points to the centre, which is the opposite. Of the rest, which one names the outer part of the town itself, rather than a line or a place outside?
items.solution:
Answer: D. edge

The fringe of a place is its outer part, the area near where it ends. Edge means the same: the outer part of something.

How to tell: the mall is on the fringe of the town, so it is inside the town but far from the centre, near where the town ends. On the edge of the town gives exactly that picture.

Why not the others:
A. limit: this is the boundary line where the town stops, and on the limit of the town is not natural English for a location.
B. outside: this means beyond the town, but a place on the fringe is still part of it.
C. middle: this is the centre, the opposite of the fringe.

Exam tip: when the marked word names a place or part of something, picture it. Choose the option that names the same part, and watch for opposites placed as traps.

items.hint1: Look at what was spurned: an offer. Ask what a person can do with an offer, and what attitude the marked word suggests.
items.hint2: To spurn an offer is to turn it down rudely or with scorn. Options that mean explaining a word, or proving a statement wrong, do not fit an offer.
items.hint3: You should be left with denied and rebuffed. Which one sits naturally with an offer, and also carries the sense of a rude refusal?
items.solution:
Answer: A. rebuffed

To spurn an offer is to reject it with scorn, as if it is not good enough. To rebuff someone or their offer is to turn it down sharply or rudely, so the two mean nearly the same.

How to tell: the supervisor turned down the cleaner's offer of help, and spurned shows it was done with contempt. The supervisor rebuffed the offer of help keeps both ideas: refusal and rudeness.

Why not the others:
B. denied: means said something is untrue, or refused to give something; it does not sit naturally with an offer and lacks the scorn.
C. defined: means explained the meaning of something, which has nothing to do with an offer.
D. refuted: means proved a claim or argument wrong; it is used for statements, not offers.

Exam tip: check what the marked verb acts on. Its partner must fit that same object naturally: offers are accepted, declined or rebuffed, while claims are denied or refuted.

items.hint1: The marked word is a time word. Ask when the finding happened compared with the searching.
items.hint2: Eventually means in the end, after a long wait or effort. An option about whether something is true, rather than about time, cannot fit.
items.hint3: Lately points to something recent, not to the end of a wait, so that one is out. Between presently and finally, only one also means at last, after trying or waiting. Which one is it?
items.solution:
Answer: D. finally

Eventually means in the end, after a delay or a long effort. Finally means the same: at last, after waiting or trying.

How to tell: the sentence suggests the speaker searched for the book for some time before finding it. I have finally found the book keeps that idea of at last.

Why not the others:
A. actually: means in fact, which is about truth, not time.
B. lately: means recently, in the recent past, not at last after a long search.
C. presently: means soon, or now, which does not look back at a wait.

Exam tip: for time words, pin down exactly when: recently, now, soon, or at the end of a wait. Words like eventually and presently are common traps because they look alike but mean different things.

items.hint1: Think of words in the same family as the marked word, such as inquire, which means to ask.
items.hint2: Inquisitive is about wanting to know things. It is not a word for bad behaviour, even though the sentence says too much of it is not good.
items.hint3: Two options are left, playful and curious. Which one is about the wish to find things out, rather than having fun?
items.solution:
Answer: C. curious

An inquisitive person wants to know things and asks many questions. Curious means the same: eager to find out or learn.

How to tell: the word comes from the same family as inquire and inquiry, which are about asking. The sentence warns against a child being too eager to know things. It is not good for a child to be unduly curious keeps that meaning.

Why not the others:
A. naughty: means badly behaved; the sentence says too much inquisitiveness is not good, but that does not make the word mean naughty.
B. playful: means fond of games and fun, not of finding things out.
D. troublesome: means causing trouble, which again describes behaviour, not the wish to know.

Exam tip: do not let the tone of the sentence choose for you. Words such as not good pull you towards negative options, but the marked word's own meaning decides. Word families (inquire, inquiry, inquisitive) are a strong clue.

items.hint1: The part of the sentence after the semicolon gives an example of the marked word. Use it as a clue.
items.hint2: Jumping off high fences is risky. Audacious describes a person who is bold enough to take risks. Being clever does not fit that example.
items.hint3: Active, agile and daring could all describe someone who jumps. Ask which one is about the courage to take a risk, rather than energy or quick, light movement.
items.solution:
Answer: A. daring

An audacious person is bold and willing to take risks that others would avoid. Daring means the same: brave enough to do dangerous or risky things.

How to tell: the example after the semicolon, jumping off high fences, shows a person taking a risk. Kofi is rather daring fits that example exactly.

Why not the others:
B. smart: means clever, or well dressed, but the example is about risk, not brains.
C. active: means lively and always doing things, and an active boy need not take risks.
D. agile: means able to move quickly and easily, which is a skill, not boldness.

Exam tip: when the words after a semicolon, or after 'for example', give an example of the marked word, use that example to test the options. Choose the option that the example proves, not one it merely allows.

items.hint1: The marked word describes the way the criminal came towards the people. Think about how the crowd would feel as they watched.
items.hint2: Menacingly comes from menace, which means danger or possible harm. A word about moving secretly is about hiding, not about showing danger.
items.hint3: Cunningly and calculatedly are about clever or careful planning. Does the marked word tell you about the criminal's planning, or about the danger the crowd could sense?
items.solution:
Answer: D. threateningly

A menace is a danger or a threat. To act menacingly is to behave in a way that shows you may cause harm, which is what threateningly means.

How to tell: the criminal came towards the crowd in a way that made them feel in danger. The criminal approached the crowd threateningly keeps that meaning.

Why not the others:
A. stealthily: means quietly and secretly so as not to be noticed, which is about hiding, not danger.
B. cunningly: means in a clever, tricky way, which is about being sly, not threatening.
C. calculatedly: means in a carefully planned way, which is about planning, not the danger shown.

Exam tip: find the base word of the marked word, allowing for spelling changes (menace in menacingly), and match its meaning. Then make sure the option does the same job in the sentence, such as describing how an action was done.

items.hint1: Look at the verb that opens the sentence, 'He said', and the phrase 'by then' at the end. Both of them control the verb in the gap.
items.hint2: When words are reported after a past verb such as said, 'will' usually moves back to 'would'. 'By then' points to a job complete before a certain time, which the perfect form, have + past participle, shows.
items.hint3: Two options already use 'would'. Which of those two also shows the painting as finished by that time?
items.solution:
Answer: B. would have finished

When a statement is reported after a past verb such as said, its verb usually moves one step back into the past, so 'will' becomes 'would'. The phrase 'by then' points to work complete before a certain time, and the perfect form, have + past participle, shows that completion.

How to tell: his actual words were something like 'They will have finished painting the house by then.' Reported after 'He said', will have finished becomes would have finished.

Why not the others:
A. will have finished: it keeps 'will', which does not match the past verb 'said'.
C. will finish: it keeps 'will', and it drops the perfect form of the original 'will have finished'.
D. would finish: it moves back correctly but drops 'have', so it does not keep the perfect form of the original words.

Exam tip: in reported speech after said, told or asked, the usual pattern in these questions is to move each verb one step back (will → would, can → could, is → was), and to keep 'have' if the original words had a perfect form.

items.hint1: When several describing words come before a noun, English puts them in a set order. Work out what kind of detail each word gives.
items.hint2: The three words here describe age, colour and material. In the usual English order, material sits closest to the noun.
items.hint3: So 'silk' comes just before 'dress'. Of the options that end with 'silk', which one puts age before colour?
items.solution:
Answer: C. new blue silk

Adjectives before a noun follow a usual order in English: opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, purpose. Each word may be correct on its own, but the wrong order sounds odd to a fluent speaker.

How to tell: 'new' is age, 'blue' is colour and 'silk' is material. Age comes before colour, and colour before material, so: my new blue silk dress.

Why not the others:
A. blue silk new: it puts age last, after material.
B. blue new silk: it puts colour before age.
D. silk blue new: it turns the whole order backwards.

Exam tip: remember OSASCOMP (opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, purpose). Label each adjective in the options with its type, then pick the option that follows that order.

items.hint1: Look at 'If' and at 'would' in the second half. Is this something real, or something imagined?
items.hint2: A person cannot become an eagle, so this is an imagined (unreal) condition. Standard English uses a special verb form, called the subjunctive, in if-clauses like this.
items.hint3: The present forms do not suit an imagined situation. Of the two past forms, one is the ordinary past tense of 'be' with 'I'; the other is the subjunctive form, used with every subject in an unreal condition. Which is which?
items.solution:
Answer: B. were

An imagined or impossible condition uses the subjunctive mood, the verb form for wishes and things that are not real. When the verb is 'be', standard written English, and WASSCE, uses 'were' for every subject: if I were, if he were, if they were.

How to tell: the speaker is not an eagle, and 'would fly' in the second half confirms that the whole idea is imagined. So the if-clause takes 'were'.

Why not the others:
A. was: many people say it in everyday speech, but the examiner expects the subjunctive 'were' in an unreal condition.
C. am: it is present tense, which suits a real, possible condition, not an impossible one.
D. be: it is not used in an if-clause like this in modern English.

Exam tip: when an if-clause needs a form of 'be' for something untrue or impossible and the other half uses 'would', choose 'were', whatever the subject.

items.hint1: Ask yourself whether chalk is something you count one by one, or a material you treat as a mass, like water or sand.
items.hint2: In standard English, chalk in the sense of the material you write with is uncountable. Uncountable nouns do not take 'a' and do not add -s.
items.hint3: Two options wrongly add -s to 'chalk'. Of the other two, which determiner goes with an uncountable noun, as in '___ water'?
items.solution:
Answer: C. some chalk

Chalk, the material a teacher writes with, is treated as an uncountable noun in standard English. In this sense it has no plural and does not take 'a'. It takes words such as some, much or a little.

How to tell: you say 'some water', not 'a water' or 'waters'. Chalk works the same way. To count it, add a counting word: a piece of chalk, two sticks of chalk.

Why not the others:
A. chalks: it adds a plural -s to an uncountable noun.
B. a chalk: 'a' treats it as countable.
D. many chalks: 'many' goes with countable plurals, and chalk is not one here.

Exam tip: for nouns such as chalk, furniture, equipment, advice and information, look for some, much or a piece of, and reject options with a, many or a plural -s.

items.hint1: This is reported speech. Check every part of each option, not only the verb.
items.hint2: When someone's words are reported later after a past verb, the verb usually moves one step back into the past, and words tied to the time and place of speaking usually change too. Check 'here' and 'yesterday'.
items.hint3: Two options have 'had eaten'. Which of them has also changed its time word to suit reported speech?
items.solution:
Answer: A. had eaten there the previous day

When words are reported after a past verb such as said, the tense usually moves back one step, and time and place words shift away from the speaker's moment. So 'ate' becomes 'had eaten', 'here' becomes 'there' and 'yesterday' becomes 'the previous day'.

How to tell: his words were 'I ate here yesterday.'
Tense: ate → had eaten
Place: here → there
Time: yesterday → the previous day
Put together: he had eaten there the previous day.

Why not the others:
B. ate here yesterday: it keeps the verb, the place word and the time word exactly as they were spoken.
C. has eaten there before: 'has' is present perfect, which does not match the past verb 'said'.
D. had eaten there yesterday: the tense and place are right, but 'yesterday' has not been changed.

Exam tip: in reported speech questions, check the verb first, then every time and place word. Common shifts: today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, yesterday → the previous day, now → then, here → there.

items.hint1: The sentence is about health. Think of the phrase used in Biology and Home Economics for healthy eating.
items.hint2: The word must describe a diet that has each class of food in the right amounts. 'Delicious' is about taste, not health.
items.hint3: Mixed and complete talk about variety or amount. Which remaining word suggests the right proportions, the way a pair of scales is held level?
items.solution:
Answer: A. balanced

A balanced diet is the set term for meals that contain each class of food, such as carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals and water, in the right proportions. In English some words simply go together, and this pair is one of them.

How to tell: the sentence links the diet to being healthy. The word that carries that health meaning with 'diet' is balanced.

Why not the others:
B. complete: it is not the set phrase, and it does not say the amounts are in proportion.
C. mixed: a mixed diet has variety, but it could still have too much of one food.
D. delicious: it describes taste, which says nothing about health.

Exam tip: in word-choice questions, look for the word the subject area normally pairs with the noun. Health: balanced diet. Weather: heavy rain. Money: sound investment.

items.hint1: This is a phrasal verb: a verb plus a small word that together take a new meaning. Think about what someone does with an omelette.
items.hint2: The meaning needed is 'prepare quickly, from whatever is at hand'. 'Rustle on' is not an English phrasal verb at all.
items.hint3: Of what remains, which particle also goes with cook and whip when they mean making food quickly: cook ___ a meal, whip ___ a snack?
items.solution:
Answer: B. up

'Rustle up' is a phrasal verb meaning to prepare a meal quickly from whatever is available. The particle 'up' appears in several verbs about producing something quickly, such as whip up and cook up.

How to tell: the speaker is being modest. They may not cook a feast, but they can at least make an omelette quickly. That is rustle up.

Why not the others:
A. out: 'rustle out' is not an English phrasal verb with this meaning.
C. on: 'rustle on' is not an English phrasal verb.
D. off: 'rustle off' is not an English phrasal verb with this meaning.

Exam tip: when the gap is a particle after a verb, test each one against the sense of the whole sentence. For making food quickly, 'up' is the usual particle: rustle up, whip up, cook up.

items.hint1: The gap sits before an adjective, 'unhappy'. Think about which words can make an adjective stronger, and what, if anything, each one needs after it.
items.hint2: 'Such' goes before a noun (such a sad boy), and 'much' is used before comparatives (much happier), not before a plain adjective like 'unhappy'.
items.hint3: That leaves two words. One simply makes the adjective stronger. The other means 'more than is right or wanted'. Which meaning does the sentence need?
items.solution:
Answer: A. very

'Very' is the plain intensifier: it makes an adjective stronger and needs nothing after it. 'Too' means 'more than is right or wanted', and it is often followed by a result: too unhappy to eat, too tired for games.

How to tell: the sentence simply says how unhappy Banku was after the fight. It does not say he was more unhappy than he should have been, and no result follows, so 'very' fits.

Why not the others:
B. too: some people use it in everyday speech to mean 'very', but in standard English it signals excess, more than is right, which the sentence does not suggest.
C. much: it strengthens comparatives (much sadder) but does not normally sit before a plain adjective like 'unhappy'.
D. such: it goes before a noun phrase, as in 'such an unhappy boy', not before an adjective on its own.

Exam tip: choose 'very' for a high degree and 'too' for more than is right or wanted. A result such as 'to eat' or 'for games' after the adjective is a strong sign of 'too'.

items.hint1: Look at 'cheaper'. Is it a plain adjective, a comparative or a superlative? That decides which words can go before it.
items.hint2: 'Cheaper' is a comparative. 'Most' forms superlatives (most expensive), so it cannot sit in front of a word that is already comparative. 'Strongly' goes with verbs of feeling or belief, as in 'strongly agree'.
items.hint3: Between the two words left, which one do English speakers normally put before a comparative adjective, as in '___ bigger' or '___ better'?
items.solution:
Answer: B. considerably

Comparative adjectives such as cheaper, bigger and better are strengthened by adverbs of degree like much, far, a lot and considerably. 'Considerably' means 'by a large amount', which fits the price drop in a sale.

How to tell: 'cheaper' is comparative, so the gap needs an adverb that normally goes before comparatives. 'Considerably cheaper' is the natural pairing.

Why not the others:
A. greatly: it usually goes with verbs and past participles (greatly improved, greatly admired), not before a comparative adjective like 'cheaper'.
C. strongly: it goes with verbs of feeling and belief (strongly agree), not with price.
D. most: it forms superlatives, and 'most cheaper' doubles up the comparison.

Exam tip: before a comparative (an -er word or more + adjective), the safe intensifiers are much, far, a lot, considerably and significantly. Reject 'most' and 'very' in that position.

items.hint1: Think about what the boot of a car is made of, and what happens to that material when something hits it.
items.hint2: A car's boot is mostly metal. 'Cracked' and 'chipped' describe damage to hard, brittle things such as glass, plates or paint.
items.hint3: Of the two words left, one describes metal pushed inward by a blow and the other a light stain or scratch. Which suits an accident?
items.solution:
Answer: B. dented

A dent is a hollow pushed into a surface by a blow. It is the usual word for damage to metal bodywork, such as a car door, bonnet or boot, after a knock or crash.

How to tell: the boot is metal and it was damaged in an accident. Metal that is hit hard bends inward rather than breaking, so it is dented.

Why not the others:
A. cracked: it is used for brittle things like glass, a windscreen or a wall, which split rather than bend.
C. chipped: it means a small piece has broken off an edge, as with paint, a plate or a tooth.
D. marked: it means stained or lightly scratched, which is too mild for accident damage.

Exam tip: match the damage word to the material. Metal gets dented, glass gets cracked or shattered, paint and china get chipped, cloth gets torn.

items.hint1: The gap follows the noun 'environment' and opens a clause that describes it. What kind of word links a noun to a describing clause?
items.hint2: This needs a relative pronoun. 'What' does not follow a noun in this way: you would not say 'the house what I live in'.
items.hint3: The children grow inside the environment. Remember that 'that' cannot come straight after a preposition in a describing clause. Of the options left, which one gives the right preposition for growing inside a place?
items.solution:
Answer: A. in which

A relative clause describes a noun and is opened by a relative pronoun such as who, which or that. When the idea needs a preposition (the children grow in the environment), the preposition can go in front of 'which': in which.

How to tell: turn the clause back into a sentence: 'Their children can grow in the environment.' Replace 'the environment' with 'which' and move 'in which' to the front: 'an environment in which their children can grow'.

Why not the others:
B. what: it does not refer back to a noun, so it cannot follow 'environment'.
C. from where: it means 'starting from that place', which is the wrong sense for growing inside an environment.
D. in that: 'that' cannot come straight after a preposition in a relative clause, and 'in that' on its own means 'because' or 'to the extent that'.

Exam tip: to test a relative clause, rewrite it as a full sentence and see which preposition the verb needs. Then put that preposition before which (or whom for people).

items.hint1: Look at the words 'cannot ___ admire'. The gap, together with 'cannot', makes a fixed expression.
items.hint2: The fixed expression means 'cannot help admiring' or 'have no choice except to admire'. 'Though' and 'however' join or contrast whole clauses, so they cannot sit between 'cannot' and a verb.
items.hint3: Of the two short words left, which one can also mean 'except', as in 'nothing ___ the truth'?
items.solution:
Answer: C. but

'Cannot but' followed by a plain verb is a fixed, formal expression meaning 'cannot help doing' or 'have no choice except to'. Here 'but' carries its older meaning, 'except'.

How to tell: the sentence sets their shortcomings against our feelings. Whatever their faults, we cannot help admiring them. So: we cannot but admire them.

Why not the others:
A. yet: 'cannot yet admire' would mean 'not now, maybe later', which loses the sense of the sentence.
B. though: it links a clause of contrast and cannot sit between 'cannot' and 'admire'.
D. however: it links sentences or clauses and makes no sense between 'cannot' and 'admire'.

Exam tip: when you see 'cannot ___' followed by a plain verb, test 'cannot but'. It means the same as 'cannot help' + -ing: cannot but admire = cannot help admiring.

items.hint1: The subject is a plan. Think about the phrasal verbs made with 'fall' and what each one means.
items.hint2: Something went wrong with the plan 'at the last moment'. 'Fell on' is used for a date or a duty (Christmas fell on a Monday), so it does not fit.
items.hint3: Of the three left, which one means that an arrangement failed and did not happen, and which ones are about dropping or getting less?
items.solution:
Answer: C. fell through

'Fall through' is a phrasal verb meaning that a plan, deal or arrangement fails and does not happen.

How to tell: plans and deals fall through. 'At the last moment' tells you it collapsed just before it was due to happen.

Why not the others:
A. fell down: it is mostly used for things that drop to the ground, or for an argument with a weak point, not for a plan that did not happen.
B. fell on: it is used for a day or date (my birthday fell on a Sunday) or a duty landing on someone.
D. fell off: it means dropped from something, or became less (sales fell off).

Exam tip: link each phrasal verb to its usual subject. Plans and deals fall through, sales fall off, friends fall out (quarrel).

items.hint1: A question tag copies the helping verb and subject of one clause. First find which clause is the main one in this sentence.
items.hint2: When one clause reports what someone thinks or says, the tag usually follows the main clause (the person thinking), not the thought inside it. A positive main clause takes a negative tag.
items.hint3: The main clause here has no helping verb of its own, so the tag must borrow one, as in 'You like rice, ___ you?'. Which option does that with the right subject?
items.solution:
Answer: B. don’t you

A question tag repeats the helping verb and the subject of the main clause, turning positive into negative or negative into positive. When the main clause has no helping verb, the tag uses do, does or did.

How to tell: the main clause is 'You think'. 'I am hungry' is only the thing thought. 'You think' is positive with no helping verb, so the tag is negative with do: You think I am hungry, don’t you?

Why not the others:
A. am I: it tags 'I am hungry' instead of 'You think', and it is positive after a positive statement.
C. aren’t I: it would be the tag for 'I am hungry' on its own, but here that clause is not the main one.
D. isn’t i: 'isn’t' does not go with 'I', and it also tags the wrong clause.

Exam tip: when a sentence starts with 'You think', 'You know' or 'He said', tag that first clause: You know he is rich, don’t you? Check the helping verb, the subject and positive or negative.

items.hint1: The object is 'tears'. Think about the phrase for suddenly starting to cry.
items.hint2: The phrase must mean 'began suddenly'. 'Broke to' is not an English phrasal verb, and 'broke with' means ended a friendship or stopped following a tradition.
items.hint3: Two options remain. One is about something ending or separating. The other is about entering a new state suddenly. Which one suits crying?
items.solution:
Answer: D. broke into

'Break into' can mean to start doing something suddenly: break into tears, break into song, break into a run. 'Burst into tears' is the more common phrase with the same meaning.

How to tell: the bad news made Maria start crying at once. That sudden start is 'broke into tears'.

Why not the others:
A. broke to: it is not an English phrasal verb.
B. broke up: it means a relationship ended, a crowd or meeting scattered, or school closed for the holidays.
C. broke with: it means ended a link with someone or stopped following a tradition.

Exam tip: 'into' after break or burst marks a sudden start of a new state or action: burst into flames, broke into laughter. Use that idea when the object is a feeling or an activity.

items.hint1: Look at 'before I arrived'. Two past actions are involved. Which one happened first?
items.hint2: An action finished before another past action takes the past perfect: had + past participle. Also check that each option is correctly formed.
items.hint3: Two options are broken in form. Of the other two, one ties the eating to the present moment and one places it in the past, before 'arrived'. Which order of events does the sentence need?
items.solution:
Answer: B. had eaten

The past perfect (had + past participle) shows that one past action was already finished before another past action. It lets the reader see the order of events.

How to tell: the arrival is in the simple past. The eating came earlier, so it goes one step further back: Jide had eaten before I arrived.

Why not the others:
A. could have eat: after 'could have', the verb must be the past participle 'eaten', so this is wrong in form.
C. must had eaten: after a modal such as 'must', the next verb stays in its base form: must have eaten, not must had.
D. have eaten: this is present perfect, and it does not agree with the singular subject Jide, which would need 'has'.

Exam tip: when a sentence has 'before', 'after' or 'by the time' with a simple past verb, put the earlier action in had + past participle.

items.hint1: The sentence sets up a contrast with 'but'. What does that tell you about how much he really knew?
items.hint2: The gap completes a fixed expression, 'next to ___', meaning 'almost ___'. Since he only claimed to be an expert, the phrase must show he knew very little.
items.hint3: Two options would say he knew a lot or a fair amount, which does not contrast with the claim. Of the other two, which makes the fixed phrase meaning 'almost none'?
items.solution:
Answer: B. nothing

'Next to nothing' is a fixed expression meaning 'almost nothing' or 'very little'.

How to tell: 'but' shows a contrast. He claimed to be an expert, but in fact he knew next to nothing, that is, very little.

Why not the others:
A. everything: 'next to everything' is not a fixed phrase, and knowing everything would not contrast with the claim.
C. something: 'next to something' makes no sense in this frame.
D. anything: 'next to anything' is not the fixed phrase; with 'anything' you would say 'hardly anything'.

Exam tip: when the gap completes a set phrase, the small words cannot be swapped. Learn such phrases as whole units: next to nothing, all but, cannot but, for good.

items.hint1: The opening phrase comes before the main clause and tells you what he did first. Look at the order of the two actions.
items.hint2: The buying was complete before he gave the advice. A finished earlier action in an opening phrase uses the perfect participle: having + past participle.
items.hint3: Two options put an -ing verb straight after 'having', which is not correct English. Of the other two, which shows a finished action rather than one still going on?
items.solution:
Answer: B. having bought

The perfect participle, having + past participle, shows that one action was completed before the action in the main clause. It often opens a sentence: Having finished her work, she went out.

How to tell: first he bought the textbooks, then he advised his daughter. The buying is complete, so: Having bought the textbooks, he advised his daughter.

Why not the others:
A. having being to buy: 'having being' is not a correct form, and 'to buy' shows no completed action.
C. having buying: after 'having', the verb must be a past participle, not an -ing form.
D. having been buying: it shows an action going on over a period, not one completed before the advice.

Exam tip: if an opening phrase describes something done before the main action, choose having + past participle (having eaten, having seen, having bought).

items.hint1: The gap follows the noun 'deficiency'. Many nouns are paired with a particular preposition.
items.hint2: A deficiency is a lack of something your body needs. 'From' shows a source and 'for' shows a purpose, so neither introduces the thing that is lacking.
items.hint3: Compare 'rich ___ vitamins' and 'low ___ fat'. Is the preposition that fits those phrases 'on', or the other option left?
items.solution:
Answer: B. in

The noun 'deficiency', meaning a lack of something needed, is commonly followed by 'in': a deficiency in iron, a deficiency in vitamin C. The adjective 'deficient' takes 'in' as well. (You may also meet 'a deficiency of', but 'of' is not among the options.)

How to tell: 'deficiency in just one essential vitamin' names the thing that is lacking.

Why not the others:
A. on: 'deficiency on' is not used; 'on' is for surfaces or topics.
C. from: it shows a source, as in 'suffering from', not the thing that is lacking.
D. for: it shows purpose or reason, not what is missing.

Exam tip: learn nouns together with their prepositions: deficiency in, interest in, lack of, need for, reason for. When unsure, test the matching adjective too: deficient in, rich in.

items.hint1: Look at 'the' just before the gap and at 'since joining the class'. The sentence compares this time with every other time.
items.hint2: Comparing one thing with every other member of a group calls for the superlative form (-est or most). 'Lately' means 'recently', which makes no sense after 'the'.
items.hint3: 'Early' is the plain form and 'later' is a comparative, which sets two things side by side. Which option compares this one submission with all the others?
items.solution:
Answer: C. earliest

The superlative (-est or most) compares one thing with every other member of a group. 'The + superlative + since ...' is a common pattern: the best film I have seen since January.

How to tell: this submission is compared with all his other submissions since he joined the class. That needs the superlative of early: the earliest.

Why not the others:
A. early: the plain form does not compare, and 'the early he has submitted' is not English.
B. later: a comparative sets two things side by side, usually with 'than', not one against a whole group.
D. lately: it is an adverb meaning 'recently', which does not fit after 'the'.

Exam tip: 'the' before the gap plus a phrase such as 'since', 'ever', 'of all' or 'in the class' is a strong signal for the superlative.

items.hint1: The sentence contrasts managing with what you have against borrowing. Think about which 'make' phrase means managing without getting more.
items.hint2: The gap is followed by 'with what one has', so the phrase must go with 'with' and mean 'manage'. 'Make over' means to hand property to someone or to change how something looks.
items.hint3: Try each remaining phrase in this sentence: 'I will ___ with this old phone until I can afford a new one.' Which one sounds right?
items.solution:
Answer: C. make do

'Make do (with something)' means to manage with what you have, even if it is not ideal.

How to tell: the sentence advises using 'what one has rather than' borrowing more. That is making do with it.

Why not the others:
A. make up: it means to invent a story, to become friends again, or to form a whole, not to manage with little.
B. make out: it means to see, hear or understand something with difficulty.
D. make over: it means to hand property over to someone or to change how something looks.

Exam tip: the words after the gap often point to the right phrasal verb. 'Make do' goes with 'with', 'make up' often with 'for' (make up for lost time), and 'make out' with something you can barely see or understand.

items.hint1: The gap comes before the plain adjective 'hasty'. Think about which words can come before an adjective to show how much.
items.hint2: 'Much' is not normally used before a plain adjective like 'hasty'; it goes before comparatives, as in 'much faster'. 'More' makes a comparison and needs something to compare with.
items.hint3: Of the two left, one means 'rather' or 'a little' and the other means 'hardly'. Which one fits a comment on how the teacher punished?
items.solution:
Answer: D. somewhat

'Somewhat' is an adverb of degree meaning 'rather' or 'to some extent'. It sits naturally before a plain adjective: somewhat hasty, somewhat tired.

How to tell: the sentence makes a mild criticism: the teacher punished a little too quickly. 'Somewhat hasty' says exactly that.

Why not the others:
A. more: it makes a comparison, so it needs something to compare with, usually after 'than', which the sentence does not give.
B. much: it is not standard before a plain adjective like 'hasty'; it strengthens comparatives such as 'much hastier'.
C. scarcely: it means 'hardly', which is an odd way to describe how someone acts and misses the criticism in the sentence.

Exam tip: before a plain adjective, safe degree words are very, rather, quite, fairly and somewhat. Keep much and far for comparatives, and check that 'more' has something to compare with.

items.hint1: A question tag needs the right helping verb, the right pronoun, and the opposite sense (positive or negative) to the statement. Check all three.
items.hint2: The statement uses 'should' and is positive, so the tag must be negative. That rules out two options.
